\chapter{How Tall, How Long, How Full}
\label{ch:alto-y-largo}
\hlchaptermodality{365}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say alto, largo, ancho, corto and lleno, and put a measurement on a thing in words rather than numbers.}

Complete ES-C365-lleno: describe a thing by height, length, width and how much is in it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[alto]{alto — high, and deep as well}

\label{lesson:ES-C365-alto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the finger}, then \emph{the heart}. (\emph{El dedo}; \emph{el corazón}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la montaña — the tallest thing you have named so far, and the first thing you will call \emph{alto}.
  \item grande — the size word you already own, so you can feel where \emph{alto} is narrower than it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{AL-to}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{l} is light and forward, never swallowed the way an English \emph{l} is at the end of \emph{tall}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{alto} — \textquotedblleft{}high, tall.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{altus} meant high. It also meant deep. A Roman writer could use the one adjective for a tower and for a trench in the sea, because \emph{altus} measured how far a thing ran along the up-down line without saying which end you were standing at. Spanish kept the upward half. English kept a memory of the other half in \textbf{the high seas}, which are not tall.

English owns the word several times over, and by several doors:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{altitude} came straight across from the Latin;
  \item to \textbf{exalt} is to raise a thing up;
  \item \textbf{enhance} arrived through Old French \emph{enhaucier}, from a late Latin \emph{inaltiāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to make higher\textquotedblright{};
  \item \textbf{haughty} is French \emph{haut}, \textquotedblleft{}high\textquotedblright{}, with an English \emph{-gh-} pushed in centuries later by scribes who liked the look of it. Someone haughty is carrying their head high.
\end{itemize}

The prettiest one is an instrument. French named a woodwind \emph{hautbois} — \emph{haut} \textquotedblleft{}high\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{bois} \textquotedblleft{}wood\textquotedblright{}, the high-pitched one. English borrowed that word once, as \textbf{hautboy}. Then it borrowed the same word a second time, after the Italians had respelled it, and that second helping is the \textbf{oboe} in every orchestra. One French word, two doors, two English words.

Carry one warning. If someone shouts \textbf{¡Alto!} at you in Spanish it means \textquotedblleft{}Stop!\textquotedblright{} — and that is not this word. It came in from Germanic by way of Italian, a relative of German \emph{halt}. Two spellings alike, two families.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say how tall a thing stands: \emph{alto}, and \emph{muy alto} when it towers.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{alto}
  \item \emph{muy alto}
  \item \emph{el árbol es alto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two directions did Latin \emph{altus} cover? (High and deep.) And what is an \emph{oboe} taken apart? (French \emph{hautbois}, high wood.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[largo]{largo — the false friend that means long}

\label{lesson:ES-C365-largo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the heart}, then \emph{tall}. (\emph{El corazón}; \emph{alto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el metro — the unit you measure a \emph{largo} thing in.
  \item el camino — the first noun most learners want to call \emph{largo}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{LAR-go}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} is one flick of the tongue, and the \emph{g} is hard, the \emph{g} of \emph{gato}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{largo} — \textquotedblleft{}long.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{largus} did not mean big, and it did not mean long. It meant \textbf{abundant, open-handed, generous}. A \emph{largus} host poured freely.

That adjective went into Old French, and out of Old French into English as \textbf{large}. Watch what English did with it. Abundant became broad. Broad became big. Today \emph{large} is the plain word for size, and nothing about it sounds generous any more — except in one fossil, \textbf{largesse}, money or favour handed out lavishly. That fossil is how we know where the word began.

Spanish took the very same adjective down a different road. Abundant became extended; extended became \textbf{long}. Spanish already had an inherited word for long, \emph{luengo}, worn down from Latin \emph{longus}, and \emph{largo} elbowed it so far aside that \emph{luengo} now sounds like something out of an old ballad.

One Latin adjective, two languages, two narrowings — and a trap that catches most beginners. \textbf{Una casa larga} is a house that runs back a long way. A large house is \textbf{una casa grande}. Reach for \emph{largo} when you mean big and your listener will picture a corridor.

(English \textbf{grand} is Latin \emph{grandis}, which has done its own drifting, from full-grown to imposing.)

Musicians know the word already without knowing it. A passage marked \textbf{largo} is played slowly, stretched out — long.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now call a thing long without accidentally calling it big: \emph{largo} for length, \emph{grande} for size.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{largo}
  \item \emph{muy largo}
  \item \emph{el camino es largo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{largus} actually mean? (Abundant, generous.) And which English word still keeps that older sense? (\emph{Largesse}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ancho]{ancho — one Latin word that arrived twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C365-ancho}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{tall}, then \emph{long}. (\emph{Alto}; \emph{largo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la calle — streets are the thing you most often call \emph{ancha}.
  \item la puerta — a doorway is where width stops being an abstraction.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{AN-cho}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ch} is the sound in English \emph{church} — never a \emph{k}, never a \emph{sh}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ancho} — \textquotedblleft{}wide.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{amplus} meant spacious, roomy, ample. English has the borrowed branch of this family and uses it constantly: something \textbf{ample} is generous in size, to \textbf{amplify} is \emph{amplus} plus \emph{facere}, \textquotedblleft{}to make roomy\textquotedblright{}, and the \textbf{amplitude} of a wave is how much room the wave takes up.

Spanish has that borrowed branch too. But Spanish also has the word the hard way, worn thin by centuries of people saying it out loud. The middle of \emph{amplus} is a pile of three consonants, \emph{-mpl-}, and that pile did not survive the journey. What came out at the far end was \textbf{ancho}. Latin \emph{īnflāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to blow into\textquotedblright{}, came out as \emph{hinchar}, \textquotedblleft{}to swell\textquotedblright{} — the same pile, the same landing.

Then something worth pausing on. Long after \emph{ancho} had settled into everyday speech, scholars reading Latin reached back and pulled \emph{amplus} into Spanish a second time, this time off the page rather than out of a mouth. That second helping is \textbf{amplio}, and it is still in use, in a more bookish register.

So Spanish holds one Latin adjective in two shapes at once: one that walked in and one that was carried in. Nothing demonstrates more cleanly that a word is shaped by the road it took.

A caution for the ear. \textbf{Ancla}, an anchor, is Greek \emph{ankyra}. \textbf{Anchoa}, an anchovy, is something else again. Three Spanish words opening \emph{anch-}, three unrelated families.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now measure a thing across as well as up and along: \emph{alto}, \emph{largo}, \emph{ancho}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ancho}
  \item \emph{muy ancho}
  \item \emph{la calle es ancha}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin adjective is behind \emph{ancho}? (\emph{Amplus}, spacious.) And why does Spanish also have \emph{amplio}? (It was taken from Latin a second time, straight off the page.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[corto]{corto — short, meaning cut off}

\label{lesson:ES-C365-corto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{long}, then \emph{wide}. (\emph{Largo}; \emph{ancho}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el rato — a short while is where a beginner first needs \emph{corto}.
  \item la hora — the unit that makes a \emph{rato corto} mean something.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KOR-to}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} is a hard \emph{k} and the \emph{r} is a single tap against the ridge behind the teeth. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{corto} — \textquotedblleft{}short.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{curtus} meant cut off, docked, shortened. It described a thing that had been trimmed, not a thing born small — and Spanish kept both halves of that idea, because \emph{cortar}, \textquotedblleft{}to cut\textquotedblright{}, stands right beside \emph{corto} in the language.

English has two descendants, and both repay a look:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{curt} is the same adjective with its manners soured. It began as plain \textquotedblleft{}short\textquotedblright{} and hardened into \textquotedblleft{}so short it is rude.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{curtail} came in from Middle French \emph{courtault}, a horse whose tail had been docked. English then bent the spelling toward \textbf{tail} — a folk guess that happened to land near the truth, since a tail was exactly what got cut. The spelling is telling a story the word's own history never authorised.
\end{itemize}

Now the words you would swear belong here and do not. English \textbf{short}, \textbf{shirt} and \textbf{skirt} are Germanic to the bone: Old English \emph{sceort}, Old English \emph{scyrte}, Old Norse \emph{skyrta}. They meet \emph{curtus} only far back, at a reconstructed old root for cutting. Distant relatives, not the same word. (\textbf{Shirt} and \textbf{skirt} are worth a moment on their own: one Germanic word that entered English twice, once natively and once from Norse, and then split into the garment above and the garment below.)

One trap left. \textbf{El corte}, a cut, belongs to \emph{curtus}. \textbf{La corte}, a royal court, is Latin \emph{cohors}, and gives English \emph{court}, \emph{cohort} and \emph{courtesy}. Same letters, different gender, different family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now put a length at either end: \emph{largo} when it runs on, \emph{corto} when it stops early.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{corto}
  \item \emph{un rato corto}
  \item \emph{el camino es corto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{curtus} mean? (Cut off, docked.) And is English \emph{short} the same word? (No — it is Germanic, a distant relative at best.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lleno]{lleno — full, with its front end changed}

\label{lesson:ES-C365-lleno}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{wide}, then \emph{short}. (\emph{Ancho}; \emph{corto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la taza — a cup is the first thing you will call \emph{llena}.
  \item el vaso — and a glass is the second — \emph{el vaso está lleno}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{YE-no}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ll} is a \emph{y}, and the \emph{e} stays pure, with no glide sliding off the end of it. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lleno} — \textquotedblleft{}full.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{plēnus} meant full. Say \emph{plēnus}, then say \emph{lleno}, and you can hear what became of the front of the word: the \emph{pl-} softened into the sound Spanish spells \emph{ll}. It happened to a small crowd of words together. \emph{Plūvia}, rain, came out as \emph{lluvia}. \emph{Plōrāre}, to weep, came out as \emph{llorar}. \emph{Flamma}, a flame, came out as \emph{llama}. \emph{Clāvis}, a key, came out as \emph{llave}. Hear those four in a row and the shape of the thing arrives on its own.

English holds the other side of the family, the borrowed side:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{plenty}, \textbf{plenary} and \textbf{replenish} are all fullness;
  \item \textbf{complete} is \emph{complēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to fill up\textquotedblright{} — a complete thing has been filled;
  \item \textbf{complement}, \textbf{supplement} and \textbf{deplete} are still filling or emptying.
\end{itemize}

And the inherited cousin, the one English never needed to borrow because it already had it, is \textbf{full}. A Latin \emph{p} facing an English \emph{f}, the same pairing you get in \emph{pater} and \emph{father}.

Here is the trap. English \textbf{comply} looks like a sibling of \emph{apply}, \emph{imply} and \emph{reply}. Those three come from \emph{plicāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to fold\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Comply} does not. It comes from \emph{complēre}, filling, reaching English by way of Italian and of Spanish \emph{cumplir}. To comply is to fulfil. Two families that resemble each other only in English spelling.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a container has nothing left to add: \emph{el vaso está lleno}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lleno}
  \item \emph{el vaso está lleno}
  \item \emph{la taza está llena}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word lies under \emph{lleno}? (\emph{Plēnus}, full.) And which English word for filling hides among the folding words? (\emph{Comply} — from \emph{complēre}, not \emph{plicāre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
